newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr flounders as rate tide rolls in.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr flounders as rate tide rolls in.

text.p: A floundering Australian dollar kept its head above 75 cent support Friday but failed to make any capital out of a Reserve Bank decision not to cut rates, suggesting its troubles were far from over.

The RBA silence made many think the bank was on hold until its next board meeting on July 1, particularly as there was almost no domestic economic data of note until then. But that did not mean the market could relax as the Bank had caught everyone napping with three of its four cuts this cycle.
This was not the sort of atmosphere conducive to recovery and dealers expected a test of 75 cents and even US$.7450 soon.
The dollar was still a cent down on the week, however, and almost three cents off from the US$0.7780 level held before the RBA last cut rates on May 23.

Chart watchers had turned deeply bearish after the break of US$0.7550, which had previously been the 1997-low, and saw little to prevent the downtrend extending to the 1996 trough of 73 cents in the medium term.
The recapture of US$0.7550 was a minimum needed to prevent this and only a break above US$0.7630 would reverse the trend.
On the crosses the dollar continued to track every twitch in US$/yen, although today the currencies were relatively dull.
The local unit stood steady at 85.90/00 yen from 85.74/84 late here Thursday and a low around 83.80 jusat two days ago.
In trade weighted terms it was unchanged at 57.1.

The money market was clearly gunning for an easing with the September 90-day bank bill futures contract at 94.90, implying a a rate of 5.10 percent against the present official cash rate of 5.50 percent.
A$ forwards out to three years were now trading at a premium meaning it cost exporters to hedge forward and investors were no longer rewarded for holding the currency.

This situation could be justified on purely academic grounds in that Australian inflation has been below that in the U.S. for five of the last six years, but the prejudices of investors would take longer to overcome.

There was also a risk U.S. rates would be heading higher, although a surprisingly soft U.S. retail sales report for May released overnight made it a little less likely the Federal Reserve would hike at its next meeting on July 1-2.
Even that news was double-edged for the A$ since the less the chance of a U.S. tightening the more confident the RBA may be it could cut without sending the currency into free-fall.
As if all this were not bearish enough, dealers reported increasing unease amongst offshore investors about the risk of a drought in Australia due to the El Nino weather pattern.
If this did develop into a full scale drought it was certain to eat into Australia's agricultural exports.
There was almost no domestic data of note out next week and little the week after, so the market would have to wait until retail trade on July 2 for another reading on the economy.
